The Bagrid catfish Pseudobagrus vachellii is a freshwater species that reaches a maximum body size of 42.3 centimeters [Li = 42.3 centimeters] standard length, a value that represents the ultimate standard length recorded for adult individuals in this population. Field surveys conducted across its native range indicate that fish attain this upper boundary only under favorable conditions, placing the species among the medium-sized members of the family Bagridae. In comparison to its congeners, P. vachellii exhibits a moderately extended growth trajectory, with most individuals approaching the asymptotic length after approximately five to six years. This measurement corresponds closely to the theoretical upper limit derived from length-frequency distributions sampled over multiple seasons. The standard length remains a reliable metric for assessing somatic growth in this species, as it excludes the caudal fin and therefore minimizes variation associated with fin damage. Researchers have noted that the largest recorded individuals are typically collected from deeper, slower-moving reaches of riverine habitats, where prey availability and stable thermal regimes may promote prolonged growth.

At the onset of sexual maturation, males and females of Pseudobagrus vachellii are characterized by a standard length of approximately 15.5 centimeters [Lp = approximately 15.5 centimeters], a threshold that marks the transition to reproductive capability. This size at puberty is reached after roughly one to two years of growth, depending on local resource conditions and water temperature. Histological examination of gonadal tissue confirms that vitellogenesis in females and spermiation in males become active at this stage, indicating readiness for the first spawning event. The body mass associated with this developmental milestone is 30.9 grams [Wwp = 30.9 grams], a value that reflects the wet weight at puberty and is derived from standard length-mass regressions specific to this species. Individuals at this size typically exhibit secondary sexual characteristics, including a slightly enlarged genital papilla in males. Comparisons with other bagrid catfishes show that the size at puberty is relatively modest, suggesting an early onset of reproductive effort that may buffer against high juvenile mortality in unpredictable environments.

This annual reproductive tactics results in a high total reproductive output that compensates for the modest size of individual offspring. The eggs are demersal and adhesive, adhering to submerged vegetation and rocky substrates where they undergo incubation. Yolk-sac larvae remain endotrophic during the first few days post-hatching, relying entirely on maternal reserves until the mouth opens and exogenous feeding commences.

Under the same thermal conditions of 9 °C [T = 9 °C], the lifespan of Pseudobagrus vachellii extends to approximately 8 years [am = approximately 8 years], a duration that encompasses multiple reproductive seasons and supports an iteroparous life history. The ultimate wet weight attained by adults reaches 590.74 grams [Wwi = 590.74 grams], a value estimated from the length-weight relationship for this species and consistent with the largest individuals collected during surveys. This asymptotic mass represents the upper limit of body growth, beyond which energy is channeled primarily into reproduction. Senescence in bagrid catfishes is not well documented, but available data indicate that reproductive output may decline after the sixth year, possibly due to the cumulative costs of gamete production and reduced foraging efficiency in older fish. The relatively long lifespan compared to other small-bodied cypriniforms suggests a life-history strategy that balances early maturation with extended reproductive windows.

This pattern likely evolved in response to the seasonal availability of food resources and stable thermal conditions in its temperate river habitat. The maximum adult body mass of roughly 591 grams [Wwi = roughly 591 grams] reveals a substantial scope for post-maturation growth, enabling females to increase fecundity with age through increased body size. Comparative data from related species in the genus Pseudobagrus indicate that such a combination of early puberty and high asymptotic mass is unusual, suggesting that P. vachellii occupies a distinct niche in which both body growth and reproductive output are maximized over a prolonged lifespan. Future studies should examine how temperature variation influences the trade-off between growth rate and age at first spawning.
